articles.title: ‘It annoys people when I eat’: Siobhán McSweeney on perfect snacks, parental pressure – and the power of being ‘a delicious fatty’
articles.summary: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast? Siobhán McSweeney is teaching me her preferred way to enjoy a packet of cheese and onion crisps.
body: McSweeney burst into the public consciousness back in 2018 with Derry Girls, a comedy series about a group of Catholic schoolgirls, set against the background of the Troubles in 1990s Northern Ireland. McSweeney won a Bafta playing the girls’ headmistress, Sister Michael – a potty-mouthed, judo-loving nun – and can count Martin Scorsese as a fan. Asked for a TV recommendation during a panel discussion in 2022, the director name-checked Derry Girls and then lifted his fist in the air in a kind of salute, exclaiming rapturously, “Those nuns!”

Since Derry Girls, the actor has made a habit of portraying slightly intimidating women. She plays the achingly sarcastic celebrity chef Della Fry in Amandaland, and hosts the Irish version of The Traitors, in which she commands a pack of wolfhounds and wears a lot of ruffs. But today, McSweeney’s short, silver‑grey hair is brushed back from her face and she is dressed casually, in trousers and a simple top. Sister Michael is always lolling back in her chair and surveying you sardonically across a desk – but the real McSweeney leans forward and asks a lot of questions.
points: The Derry Girls actor has always loved food, so who better to take over as the new presenter of the Guardian’s Comfort Eating podcast?

articles.title: Tim Dowling: why did I buy an electric car? Because I wanted a medal
articles.summary: Lunch with my agent is going nowhere, so I decide to share my latest motoring anecdote. I’m having lunch with my agent – an infrequent occurrence, because neither of us ever has any good news for the other. This lunch is no different.
body: “Sorry to make you come all this way,” she says, “but I had to be near the office today.” She hints at some complex contractual negotiations involving an author for whom, I suspect, she always has good news.
“Did you come on the tube?” she says. “Did it take for ever?”
People sometimes ask why I bought an electric car. What did I want from it? To save money? To help the environment? To guard myself against future fuel shortages, or toxic emissions, or both?

The truth is: I wanted a medal. I wanted people to see the little green rectangle on my number plate and think: there goes a great guy, doing his best; let’s slow down and give him plenty of room to pull into our lane.

articles.title: ‘Comfort in a bowl’: porridge hotter than ever as fibremaxxers get their oats
articles.summary: Humble breakfast staple at heart of trend stirred up by health concerns and hearty spoonfuls of nostalgia. The clocks may be going back in the UK this weekend, but the biggest sign winter is coming is a steaming bowl of porridge on a breakfast table.
body: A staple for centuries, porridge is traditionally made with oats, water and a pinch of salt or sugar. However, the humble dish is now experiencing its own renaissance, with the latest iterations transforming it from drab to decadent. The trend is being driven by a growing fibre-centric movement as well as by nostalgia.

On social media, recipe creators are experimenting with everything from miso versions to sour cherry and pistachio butter toppings. At 26 Grains, a central London restaurant that specialises in porridge, this month’s offering includes a five-grain porridge topped with fig and red grape jam and a dollop of whipped cream. Over at Oatis in west London, toppings range from caramelised banana and tahini to mushrooms and pesto.

Alex Hely-Hutchinson, the founder of 26 Grains, describes porridge as “comfort in a bowl”. Part of its appeal, she says, is that it allows a “moment for pause in a busy world” – plus most people know how to make it.
It is a trend that is affecting home store cupboards. Searches for organic jumbo oats at Ocado are up 98% year on year while sales of White’s jumbo oats are up 56%.

articles.title: Vogue’s Guide to All the Different Types of Sunscreen
articles.summary: Chemical, mineral, spray, stick, and more, there are a lot of sunscreens out there to protect your skin. Here, Vogue breaks down everything you need to know about all the different types of sun protection you can be using daily.
body: As someone who preaches the importance of daily sun protection to anyone who will listen, I often get asked what’s the best sunscreen I’ve ever used. I could list a few of my faves (and when pressed, I do) but I usually relay the same answer that dermatologists tell me when I ask them the same question: the best sunscreen is the one you’ll actually use everyday.

We are blessed with so many sunscreen options, it’s hard to go wrong with most of them. But how does one choose that perfect formula that will make you remember this very important step in your routine? To figure that out, there are a couple of things you have to consider. If you’re an active outdoors person, for example, you might want something that’s portable and waterproof. If you have sensitive skin, you might want something with gentle ingredients that won’t cause irritation. And on top of all of that, you’ll have to understand all the different types of sunscreen available to you.

It can be a lot, but that’s where this handy guide comes in. From chemical to mineral and all the different applications, experts break down every type of sunscreen to help you make wise skin health (and shopping) decisions. Read on below.

articles.title: 7 NYC Hotels That Make Christmas Magical for Families
articles.summary: From in-room Christmas trees to a Home Alone limo tour, these Manhattan hotels make a holiday trip with kids a lot easier (and a lot more fun).
body: There's nothing quite like New York at Christmas. When I lived in the city with my family, December was always our favorite month. We'd bundle up to see the windows on Fifth Avenue, drink hot chocolate while watching the skaters at Bryant Park, and crane our necks at the tree in Rockefeller Center. The whole city feels magical this time of year, and kids pick up on it the second they step outside.

My family and I just moved to Barcelona, but we're heading back to NYC for the holidays. And since we'll be visitors this time, I started looking for hotels that would make the trip feel extra special for my kids. It turns out that many of the city's most popular properties go big for Christmas—and plenty have kids in mind when it comes to programming. Some will set up a decorated tree in your room before you check in; others will bring Santa to the lobby, pour free hot cocoa, or hide candy canes around your room for a scavenger hunt.

After a cold afternoon of skating and window shopping, it's nice to come back to a place that feels like Christmas too. Here are the seven hotels that make Christmas special in NYC, and what each one offers for families.

articles.title: What Is Mirin? Uses, Types, and Best Substitutes
articles.summary: It brings depth to sauces and gloss to glazes. Here’s how to use it—and what to reach for when you’re out.
body: If you’ve eaten Japanese food, you’ve almost certainly tasted mirin. Alongside miso, soy sauce, dashi, and rice vinegar, the sweet rice wine is a staple of Japanese cooking. It brings richness and complexity to stocks, stews, marinades, and sauces, plus a glossy sheen to glazed dishes like teriyaki.

Mirin is often described as sweet with subtle umami, but Sonoko Sakai, author of Japanese Home Cooking, prefers the term koku. “Koku is like umami, but it gives not just flavor but aroma; you feel it with your palate, and it gives depth.”

But the type of mirin you buy matters—and the bottle your local supermarket stocks likely won’t deliver the koku Sakai describes. Hon mirin, or “true” mirin, tends to be pricey and hard to find in the US. Here’s what sets it apart, when it’s worth seeking out, and what to use when you can’t find any.

Traditional hon mirin is made from just three ingredients: glutinous rice, koji, and shochu (a Japanese distilled spirit often made from rice). During production, enzymes break down the rice’s starches into “simple sugars, mostly glucose,” explains Hiroko Shimbo, author of The Japanese Kitchen. That gives mirin a distinctive sweetness without added sugar.

body: Amusingly, Garmin's own FAQ still states that the Cirqa does not vibrate for text messages, phone calls, or other smartphone notifications. Clearly that page is now out of date, so Garmin will want to correct it. Since Garmin doesn't yet have step-by-step instructions, I tested the text-message vibrations myself. Here's how you can set up your Cirqa smart band to vibrate for calls and texts, in addition to a number of other promising updates to check out.
To receive these alerts, your band must be running firmware 4.20 or later. Here is how to get everything configured.
Update the firmware. Open your Garmin Connect app and sync your Cirqa, so the app can check for and install version 4.20 or newer.
Grant the necessary phone permissions. In your phone's settings, make sure Garmin Connect has permission to access SMS, Contacts, and Phone.

articles.title: I’ve Spent Years Tracking Nordic Wellness Trends, and This Low-Impact Finnish Ritual Is About to Take Over
articles.summary: Forget hygge and lagom, Nordic walking is the latest trend to know.
body: I can smell the embers of a Nordic trend in the making from miles away. After all, even before the Swedish ethos of lagom (optimal balance) captured the world a few years ago, I’d been unpacking this Nordic mindset around wellness and lifestyle in my storytelling for years. I would go on to write an international bestseller, Lagom, with over 15 foreign editions.

From Swedish massages to Finnish saunas, the region is synonymous with wellbeing. While Denmark gave the world hygge (intentional presence), Norway friluftsliv (open-air living), Finland sisu (grit), and Iceland birthed “Viking wellness” with hot baths and cold dips, the reality is that all Nordic cultures share these values under different names. What makes lifestyle trends from the region particularly appealing globally is the foundations on which they’re built.
points: Forget hygge and lagom, Nordic walking is the latest trend to know.

articles.title: Byredo’s Havana Tonka Is a Gourmand With a Dark Side
articles.summary: Introducing Havana Tonka, the latest extrait from Byredo's Night Veils collection. A take on a grown-up gourmand, the scent mingles tonka bean, bergamot, rum, and pink peppercorn to capture the sensuality of the Cuban capital.
body: It’s been 20 years since Byredo’s founding, and in those two decades, the once-niche Swedish fragrance brand has become a household name. From Mojave Ghost to Bal D’Afrique, its scents line the fragrance walls of the industry’s most fabulous faces, practically fly off retailers’s virtual shelves, and admittedly, help set the standard of what an indie brand could be.

Formulated as an extrait, the fragrance uses high-concentration essential oils, which naturally last longer. “The idea is to create fragrances that feel rich, expressive, and full of character, with an emphasis on the depth and complexity of the ingredients,” Epinette explains. “I love the creative freedom that comes with working in this format, where you can really push certain facets of a fragrance and create something with a strong, distinctive presence.” Per Epinette, it’s less about making the fragrance shout its presence as it enters the room and more about adding depth and richness to its overall composition.
points: Introducing Havana Tonka, the latest extrait from Byredo's Night Veils collection.
